title: Iraq Devalues Dinar 14.5% as QatarEnergy Turns to Chinese Banks for $3B
subhead: The Hormuz closure is now visibly draining Gulf state finances: Baghdad slashed the dinar's value on Wednesday to cover a swelling deficit, while QatarEnergy borrowed from four Chinese banks as its LNG exports remain blocked. Financial stress, not just shipping, is becoming the story.

sections.heading: Iraq Cuts the Dinar 14.5% as Oil Revenue Falls
sections.body:
Iraq devalued the dinar by 14.5% on Wednesday, setting the official rate at 1,520 dinars per dollar, according to Reuters. The cabinet approved the new structure on Tuesday and it took effect Wednesday, with the Finance Ministry buying dollars at 1,500 and banks selling to end-users at 1,510. The move goes beyond the 1,400-1,500 range Baghdad had reportedly been weighing for its 2027 budget, which carries spending of 217 trillion dinars and a deficit north of 40 trillion dinars.

Oil sales supply the bulk of Iraqi state revenue, and months of disrupted exports through the Strait of Hormuz have punched a hole in the budget. Economists told Reuters the devaluation is a fiscal response: it raises the dinar value of dollar oil earnings, at the cost of more expensive imports.
sections.whyItMatters: Iraq's currency move is the clearest signal yet that the Hormuz crisis is now a fiscal crisis for Gulf producers, not just a shipping problem. Devaluation is a last-resort lever — it tells you Baghdad's revenue shortfall has become unmanageable at the old peg.

sections.heading: QatarEnergy Borrows $3B from Four Chinese Banks
sections.body:
State-owned QatarEnergy secured a five-year $3 billion loan from a group of Chinese banks — Bank of China, ICBC, Agricultural Bank of China, and China Construction Bank (Asia) — Bloomberg reported Wednesday. The proceeds are for general working capital as Qatar continues to struggle to move LNG cargoes through the Strait of Hormuz.

At the end of September, QatarEnergy extended force majeure on LNG deliveries to Asia and Europe by another month, through the end of November, as cargo traffic through Hormuz remains largely blocked amid the prolonged U.S.-Iran standoff. The Chinese financing stands out because some Western investors have pulled back from the conflict zone; Beijing is filling the gap.
sections.whyItMatters: This is Gulf energy finance tilting toward China in real time. When Western capital retreats from a war zone and Chinese banks step in, the financing relationships that outlast the war are being set now.

sections.heading: IEA Meets on the G7's 100-Million-Barrel Release — Still No Numbers
sections.body:
The IEA's Governing Board held an informal meeting Wednesday to discuss the planned release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel stock, two EU diplomats told Reuters. EU representatives had already discussed specifics earlier in the day, but no volumes or timelines have been publicly agreed.

The G7 announced the 100-million-barrel release over four months on October 2, including a front-loaded diesel release within the first 20 days. It remains unclear whether these barrels are part of the 400-million-barrel release the IEA announced in the spring at the peak of the Hormuz closure — a confusion that is itself adding to market uncertainty. The plan followed days of pressure from the Trump administration on France and Germany to release diesel stocks.
sections.whyItMatters: The release is announced but not operationalized. Until volumes and timing are fixed, the market is trading on a headline rather than actual barrels — which is why physical prices stay tight even as the political messaging suggests relief is coming.

sections.heading: South Korea Bets $747 Billion on Breaking Its Fuel Habit
sections.body:
South Korea unveiled the Korea Green Transformation (K-GX) Strategy through 2035, a plan to invest as much as one quadrillion Korean won ($747 billion) in renewables, EVs, and industrial decarbonization, Reuters reported. Targets include 100 GW of renewable capacity by 2030 and electric and hydrogen vehicles exceeding 70% of new vehicle sales by 2035, plus emissions cuts in steel, cement, semiconductors, petrochemicals, and refining.

President Lee Jae Myung framed it as a shift from follower to leader: 'We must move away from the practice of chasing others and become architects and leaders of the green market ourselves.' Seoul explicitly ties the plan to energy security after the Middle East crisis forced its refiners and utilities to scramble for alternative crude and LNG supplies when cargoes were trapped in Hormuz.
sections.whyItMatters: This is one of Asia's largest oil and gas importers converting a supply shock into a structural diversification program. It is the biggest single national response yet to the Hormuz crisis on the demand side, and it will reshape Asian energy procurement for a decade.

sections.heading: Australia's High Court Blocks a Coal Expansion on Scope 3 Emissions
sections.body:
Australia's High Court ruled against the planned expansion of Mach Energy's Mount Pleasant coal mine, which sought to extend the mine's life to 2048 and add 406 million tons of production, Al Jazeera and The Straits Times reported. The court found regulators had failed to consider the project's full emissions footprint — specifically Scope 3 emissions from the coal's eventual use.

One judge said the New South Wales Independent Planning Commission failed to consider whether conditions should ensure greenhouse gas emissions are minimized, having focused only on about 2% of the project's emissions. Climate activists expect the ruling to influence future approvals for hydrocarbon projects in Australia.
sections.whyItMatters: A top court making Scope 3 emissions a legal test for project approval raises the bar for coal and gas expansion far beyond Australia. With energy security arguments being used to justify new fossil supply, this ruling pushes back with a legal precedent that could travel.

sections.heading: Uniper Sale Draws Apollo as Berlin Offloads Its Gas Champion
sections.body:
Apollo Global Management submitted a non-binding bid for German gas giant Uniper, joining a race that could value Germany's largest gas importer at around €10 billion ($11.6 billion), Reuters reported. Other bidders include Equinor, Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky's EPH, a Brookfield-Canada Pension Plan consortium, and an RWE-KKR partnership. Berlin, which owns 99.12% after a €13.5 billion bailout in 2022, is expected to decide which bidders advance within weeks.

Uniper supplies roughly 190 TWh of gas annually in Germany, holds 57 TWh of LNG regasification bookings, and operates 7.2 billion cubic meters of storage, including 5.9 bcm in Germany. Those assets are central to German gas security post-Russia.
sections.whyItMatters: The sale decides who controls the infrastructure that keeps Germany's gas system functioning. With Equinor (state-linked) and financial buyers like Apollo and KKR in the mix, the outcome shapes how much of Europe's gas backbone stays under European strategic control.

sections.heading: Iranian Oil Reaches Tajikistan, Testing Sanctions Enforcement
sections.body:
Tajikistan began receiving Iranian oil and petroleum products in late August, its Energy Ministry told the Asia-Plus news agency, per RFE/RL. Volumes, prices, and transport routes were not disclosed. Dushanbe has requested as much as 2.55 million tons annually, though that is prospective rather than current.

The route matters because Russia supplied 91.1% of Tajikistan's petroleum-product imports in the first half of 2026. The move raises questions about potential U.S. secondary sanctions for dealing with Iran, especially as Washington escalates pressure.
sections.whyItMatters: A Central Asian state buying Iranian oil is a small but concrete data point on sanctions erosion: Iran finding new land-linked buyers in Russia's own neighborhood shows enforcement limits even as Washington tightens the screws.

bottomLine: The Hormuz standoff is shifting from a shipping crisis into a financial one. Iraq devalued its currency by 14.5% because oil revenue collapsed, and QatarEnergy borrowed $3 billion from Chinese banks because its LNG can't move — two different Gulf states showing the same fiscal strain, with China positioning itself as the financier of last resort in the region. Meanwhile the G7's 100-million-barrel release remains announced but unquantified, so physical markets stay tight, and buyers are responding structurally: South Korea committed $747 billion to get off imported fuel, while Australia's top court made Scope 3 emissions a legal barrier to new coal. The conflict itself hasn't moved, but its economic and policy consequences are now compounding far beyond the Strait.
sources: Reuters, Bloomberg, OilPrice.com, IEA, Al Jazeera, The Straits Times, Asia-Plus, RFE/RL
